title: Frequency-Response Visualiser
disclaimer: EXPLORATION ONLY. Not a substitute for a verified control-design toolchain. Classical textbook methods, unverified against any certified tool; margin thresholds are unsourced defaults. Check every result independently before relying on it.
units: Canonical: rad/s, seconds, absolute magnitude, degrees. Display toggles change only what is shown.
scope: Phase 2 of 4: SISO Bode view, margins, closed-loop poles and pole-zero map in continuous or discrete time, with ZOH, Tustin (optional prewarp), forward and backward Euler discretisation, integer-sample delays, a continuous-over-discrete overlay, self-tests and exports.

discretization.prewarp: Tustin prewarp frequency in rad/s; 0 means none

conventions: Open loop L(s) = K · C(s) · G(s) · e^(−sτ) with unity negative feedback; S = 1/(1 + L), T = L/(1 + L).

Evaluated at s = jω for ω > 0 in rad/s. Magnitude and phase come from the factored form k · Π(jω − zᵢ) / Π(jω − pᵢ), so accuracy holds near lightly damped poles; phase is the continuous sum of the factor angles (atan2) minus ωτ, so it is unwrapped by continuity.
Gain crossover ω_gc: |L| = 1 (0 dB), found by a sign-change scan on the grid and refined with Brent's method on log₁₀ ω. Phase margin PM = 180° + ∠L(ω_gc), wrapped to (−180°, 180°].

Phase crossover ω_pc: ∠L = −180° + k·360°, found the same way; a finite, real negative L(0) is a phase crossover at ω = 0 and, without delay, a finite, real negative L(∞) is one at ω = ∞ (marked atInfinity in JSON, where ω is written as null). Gain margin GM = −20·log₁₀|L(ω_pc)| dB. Every crossover is reported. The smallest PM governs; the upper gain margin is the smallest GM ≥ 0 dB (gain increase to instability) and the lower gain margin the largest GM < 0 dB (gain reduction to instability). The GM check passes when the upper margin ≥ threshold and the lower margin ≤ −threshold, each where present.
Delay margin = PM (rad) / ω_gc in seconds, the smallest over crossovers with positive PM; if any gain crossover has PM ≤ 0 the delay margin is 0 s, with a message.

Ms = max|S|, Mt = max|T|, refined by golden-section search on log₁₀ ω; vector margin = 1/Ms, the minimum distance from L to −1. The closed-loop resonant peak Mr is max|T| relative to the DC gain |T(0)|, and the −3 dB bandwidth is the first frequency where |T| falls below |T(0)|/√2.

Closed-loop poles are the roots (Aberth iteration) of D_C·D_G + K·N_C·N_G; in continuous time they are available only without delay. Poles with |Re| ≤ 1e-9·max(1, |p|) are on the stability boundary and reported as marginal.

Discrete time: L(z) = K · C(z) · G(z) · z^(−d) with sample time Ts, evaluated at z = e^(jωTs) for 0 < ω ≤ π/Ts (the Nyquist frequency), with each factor angle measured from +j for a root inside the unit circle and from −r for a root r outside it, so the phase stays continuous along the arc; the grid ends exactly at π/Ts and a manual ω_max above it is clipped with a warning. Stability means |p| < 1; poles with ||p| − 1| ≤ 1e-9 are on the unit circle and reported as marginal. The delay d is a whole number of samples, applied exactly as z^(−d); because z^(−d) is rational, the closed-loop poles (roots of D·z^d + N) stay available with a delay in discrete time.

Discrete phase crossovers include ω = 0 when L(1) is finite, real and negative, and ω = π/Ts when L(−1) is finite, real and negative (z = −1 makes L real, so a crossover can sit exactly at the Nyquist frequency). The ω = ∞ crossover applies only in continuous time.

Discretisation is done in state space: each continuous block is realised in controllable canonical form (it must be proper), then Ad, Bd, Cd, Dd come from zero-order hold (exact, via the matrix exponential of [[A, B], [0, 0]]·Ts by scaling and squaring with a degree-6 Padé approximant), Tustin (s = c·(z − 1)/(z + 1) with c = 2/Ts, or c = ωp/tan(ωp·Ts/2) with prewarp frequency ωp), forward Euler (s = (z − 1)/Ts) or backward Euler (s = (z − 1)/(z·Ts)). The z-domain transfer function is det-based: den = det(zI − Ad), num = Dd·den + det(zI − Ad + Bd·Cd) − den, with characteristic polynomials from a Hessenberg reduction; leading numerator coefficients below 1e-12 of the largest are treated as round-off and dropped. The discrete poles and zeros come from the exact root maps rather than by re-rooting: Tustin z = (c + p)/(c − p) plus n − m zeros at exactly z = −1, forward Euler z = 1 + p·Ts, backward Euler z = 1/(1 − p·Ts) plus n − m zeros at exactly z = 0, and ZOH poles z = e^(p·Ts) with the zeros from the discretised numerator; num and den stay the state-space result.

When every block is discretised from s, the continuous response L(jω) (with delay d·Ts) is overlaid on the discrete one to show warping and aliasing. Straight-line asymptotes are drawn in continuous time only.
assumptions: Unity negative feedback and LTI systems, in continuous or discrete time chosen globally (no mixed sampled-data loops); SISO only in this phase (Nyquist and Nichols follow in phase 3, MIMO in phase 4).
Continuous delays are exact e^(−jωτ) in the response; no Padé approximation is used in plots. Discrete delays are integer samples; fractional delays are not supported.

Each block in discrete time is either entered directly in z or entered in s and discretised by its own method (ZOH, Tustin with optional prewarp, forward or backward Euler); presets are continuous prototypes and must be discretised.
Margin thresholds are user inputs; the pre-filled values are unsourced defaults, not requirements.
Classical control theory only; no NASA or Niu source is claimed.

sources.text: Classical frequency-response analysis (Bode, gain and phase margins, sensitivity peaks) as in standard feedback-control textbooks, e.g. G. F. Franklin, J. D. Powell, A. Emami-Naeini, Feedback Control of Dynamic Systems; S. Skogestad, I. Postlethwaite, Multivariable Feedback Control, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2005.
O. Aberth, “Iteration methods for finding all zeros of a polynomial simultaneously”, Mathematics of Computation 27 (1973) 339–344 (polynomial roots).
R. P. Brent, Algorithms for Minimization without Derivatives, Prentice-Hall, 1973 (root refinement and golden-section search).
G. F. Franklin, J. D. Powell, M. L. Workman, Digital Control of Dynamic Systems, 3rd ed., Addison-Wesley, 1998 (zero-order hold, Tustin with prewarping, Euler discretisation).
C. Moler, C. Van Loan, “Nineteen dubious ways to compute the exponential of a matrix, twenty-five years later”, SIAM Review 45 (2003) 3–49 (scaling and squaring with Padé approximation).
